title: Minimum Split Into Subarrays With GCD Greater Than One
statement:
You are given an array `nums` of positive integers. Cut it into one or more contiguous, non-empty subarrays so that every element lies in exactly one of them and, inside each subarray, the greatest common divisor of all its elements is larger than `1`.

Return the smallest number of subarrays such a cut can use. Since every value is at least `2`, a valid cut always exists.
notes:
## Intuition

A piece is valid when its elements share a factor larger than `1`. Removing elements from a valid piece keeps it valid, because the GCD of fewer numbers can only stay the same or grow. So if some optimal cut ends its first piece early, we can move that boundary to the right, as far as the GCD stays above `1`, without breaking the next piece and without adding pieces. That makes the greedy choice safe: keep extending the current piece, and start a new one only when its running GCD would drop to `1`. A dynamic program over every possible last piece also works, but costs O(n²).

## Approach

1. Start with `count = 1` piece whose running GCD `current` is `nums[0]`.
2. For each next value `nums[i]`, fold it into `current` with `gcd`.
3. If `current` becomes `1`, the value cannot join this piece: close it, add one to `count`, and start a new piece with `current = nums[i]`.
4. After the loop, `count` is the answer.

## Example 1, step by step

For `nums = [12, 6, 3, 14, 8]`: `current = 12`. Adding `6` gives `gcd(12, 6) = 6`; adding `3` gives `3`. Adding `14` gives `gcd(3, 14) = 1`, so the piece `[12, 6, 3]` closes, `count = 2` and `current = 14`. Adding `8` gives `gcd(14, 8) = 2`, still valid. The answer is `2`: `[12, 6, 3]` and `[14, 8]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log M), where M is the largest value: one Euclid GCD per element.
- Space: O(1) besides the input.

## Pitfalls

- When the GCD drops to `1`, restart from `nums[i]` itself, not from `0` or `1`: that element belongs to the new piece.
- Checking only neighbours (`gcd(nums[i - 1], nums[i]) > 1`) is not enough: in `[6, 10, 15]` every neighbouring pair shares a factor, yet all three together have GCD `1`.
- A single element is always a valid piece because every value is at least `2`, so the answer never exceeds `nums.length`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `gcd` | Euclid's greatest common divisor |
| `count` | number of pieces so far, including the open one |
| `current` | GCD of the open piece |
| `i` | index of the value being added |

narration.2: Euclid's algorithm: the GCD of a and b equals the GCD of b and a mod b.
narration.3: The first element always opens the first piece.
narration.4: The open piece's GCD is just its first value for now.
narration.6: Try to add each following value to the open piece.
narration.7: Fold the new value into the piece's running GCD.
narration.8: A GCD of 1 means this value cannot share a factor with the whole piece.
narration.9: Close the piece and open a new one.
narration.10: The new piece starts with this value alone.
narration.13: Every value is in a piece, and each piece was made as long as possible.
